publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: The insulation of electrical equipment is classified according to apparatus as follows: — Cables — Substations, Switchgear and Gas-Insulated Transmission Lines — Transformers and Liquid-Filled Equipment — Rotating Machines — Insulators and Solid Insulation Systems The material in this chapter has been abstracted from journals, reports and conference records published in Europe, England, USSR, Japan, India and North America. A complete bibliography with the publishers' addresses is included.

articleTitle: Electrification due to the separation of materials
publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: Most dielectric materials acquire an electrostatic charge when brought into contact with, and then separated from, a dissimilar material. If the contacting materials are identical, electrification is observed when the two bodies are asymmetrically rubbed together. Electrification is also obtained if a dielectric material, such as mica, is simply cleaved into two parts. Since dielectric materials are good insulators, charge accumulated on a dielectric body decays very slowly. Charge retention on dielectric materials usually represents a nuisance (shocks, dust collection, etc.) or a hazard (explosion of fuels, powders, etc.). On the other hand, the motion of small dielectric particles can be controlled via an electric field if the particles acquire an electrostatic charge by contact and separation from other materials. The ability to manipulate charged particles with an electrostatic force is utilized in the electrophotographic copying process, spray painting, and separation of ores.

articleTitle: Electro-optical effects and non-linear optical phenomena in passive media
publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: The literature on electro-optical effects, to be discussed in this chapter, includes both the electric field induced changes of refractive indices (i.e. Kerr- and Pockels-effect) as well as electric field induced changes in light absorption (electrochromic effects) in dielectrics. While the number of papers reporting the measurement of electro-optic coefficients has decreased, there has been an increase in the publications dealing with applications of well known materials for modulators, integrated optics devices etc. Since it was necessary to limit the size of this review, most of the application oriented work has only been listed in the bibliography.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: Three international low temperature conferences were held in Europe in 1978: a physics conference, an engineering conference, and a materials conference. The intended coverage of this cryogenics chapter is just about coextensive with the subject areas which were treated at these meetings, so far as they concerned dielectrics. Contributions to LT15 (1) or ICEC7 (2), the latest of two major conference series will be referred to under practically all the different subheadings of the chapter. Cryogenic space engineering was given some prominence at ICEC7 amongst the more usual topics. The ICMC symposium (3) was the first such meeting to deal exclusively with non-metallic materials at low temperatures. The major topic was low temperature structural materials, and especially composites, with thermal and electrical insulating materials as important minor topics. We shall also be referring to the proceedings of a Lattice Dynamics conference (4) and of dielectric conferences not specifically concerned with low temperatures (5,6). In this introductory section we shall draw attention to a few pertinent publications of general or miscellaneous interest before dealing with the more specialised topics.

articleTitle: Dielectric behavior and structure of gases, liquids, and solids
publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: Investigations of fundamental dielectric properties of atoms, molecules, and ions in the gaseous, liquid, and solid states constitute a major portion of the literature on dielectrics. This chapter is concerned with basic dielectric phenomena. Papers that are more appropriately discussed under the titles of other chapters have been omitted.

articleTitle: Conduction, breakdown and electronic-ionic phenomena in liquids
publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: This chapter essentially covers the behavior of dielectric liquids subjected to electric fields. The separation of sections is generally self evident but for Conduction and Electronic and Ionic Phenomena, the division is less well defined. It will be found that topics involving carrier velocity and mobility have, for the most part, been included in the conduction section.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: This chapter is concerned with various aspects of insulating films. These films, because of their many applications, continue to attract a great deal of attention. The review is based on the literature abstracted in Physics Abstracts, Electrical and Electronics Abstracts, and directly from papers published in various scientific journals.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: One of the areas of most active interest in connection with conduction in vacuum over the past year has been the behavior of vacuum arcs at high currents. The subject is of enormous practical interest to vacuum interrupter development and involves a variety of physical processes the interactions of which provide fertile ground for novel experimental and theoretical investigations. The vital question concerns the Jeckyl and Hyde character of the vacuum arc anode junction. At low currents the anode termination is diffuse and passive with the anode terminal acting largely as a charge collector over its entire exposed area. At high currents the anode end of the arc may contract causing a high concentration of energy input to the electrode surface. This transition results in severe melting and violent ejection of anode metal. A variety of investigations on this subject are discussed in the section on The Arc Anode and include such subjects as the effects of axial magnetic fields, the visual appearance of the high current arc under different ignition.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: Two hundred and twenty references have been selected for inclusion in the bibliography and 90 of these papers are chosen for discussion. In the preparation of a digest of this nature, the selection of the papers may show a bias towards the writer's limitations and special interests; the present report is no exception. Topics of ferroelectricity, pyroelectricity, piezooptics and nonlinear effects have been, in general, excluded from the bibliography as these areas are now adequately covered elsewhere. Also excluded from the bibliography are dissertations, patents, and government reports.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: The 1978 Conference on Electrical Insulation and Dielectric Phenomena (1) included a session on the Dielectric properties of Biological Systems. This session was chaired by Professor H. P. Schwan of the University of Pennsylvania and was organized by the present writer on behalf of the Dielectrics Society which co-sponsored it. The introductory paper concluded that while dielectric measurements on biological materials can be very sensitive and non-invasive they are seldom specific in a chemical or biological sense. The most important of the recent trends in dielectrics is towards combining the high sensitivity of dielectric measurements with the specificity of some other physical or chemical measurement made on the same system. There are a number of such examples to be found among the papers listed in this chapter. The most difficult overall problems are those of electrode effects with the highly conducting materials encountered and the difficulties of measuring an effective geometrical shape of the specimens. Professor R. H. Cole continues to make progress with the former problem and Professor H. A. Pohl and Dr. R. Pethig have developed dielectrophoresis techniques for measurement of the dielectric properties of biological materials, and which avoid the shape factor.

articleTitle: Tables of permittivity, dipole moment, and dielectric relaxation time
publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: These tables contain data reported in publications edited in 1977 and abstracted by chemical Abstracts in 1977 and 1978. The majority of the data cited have been taken from the original literature. In cases where the original literature was unobtainable the Chemical Abstract reference number is given parenthetically after the reference itself. References are given in Chemical Abstracts' style and where an English translation of a foreign language article exists, a parenthetical reference to the translation is given also. References to data not suitable for inclusion in tabular form are noted in supplementary reference lists which follow the appropriate tables. In these sections some references to certain pertinent reviews are also included, as are references to original articles which proved to be unobtainable at the time of compilation and for which the abstract contained insufficient information.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: In the course of this survey we have consulted more than 60 journals, conference and symposium reports originating from 16 countries. The principal sources of information were the Annual Report — Conference on Electrical Insulation and Dielectric Phenomena, published by the National Academy of Sciences, Washington, D.C., and the publications of IEEE and of IEE (London). It is eight years since the authors produced a literature survey on this topic and it is interesting to note, on the one hand, an apparent decline of interest in the problem of intrinsic electric strength and in the breakdown of thin films. On the other hand, strong interest has emerged in the effects of morphology on various aspects of the electrical breakdown of polymers. As a consequence of this growing interest and the importance of the structure of dielectric materials, especially polymers, with regard to their electrical properties, we have introduced this topic under its own heading.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: The aim of this chapter is to gather information relevant to the electrical discharges and breakdown in insulating gases. References to the vast amount of literature on gas lasers, thermonuclear plasmas, magneto-hydrodynamics, high energy physics and many of the other related technical areas that make use of gas discharges are excluded from this chapter. An attempt has been made to include in the bibliography a complete list of pertinent reference material including monoenergetic beam data, swarm data and energy distributions. The material was gathered directly from the literature and it is possible that we may have overlooked some of the relevant papers.

publicationTitle: Digest of Literature on Dielectrics Volume 42 1978
abstract: The interest in studying electrical conduction and polarization phenomena in polymers has increased since last year. Besides the classical problems of conduction, polarization and breakdown in polymeric insulators, interesting for the electric and electronic industry, new aspects are being considered by more and more research groups in the field. One of these is the application of the dielectric method, especially the depolarization technique, for studying molecular mobilities, i.e., multiple phase transitions in polymeric systems. Combined with mechanical relaxation, thermal analysis, magnetic resonance and with some additional techniques dielectric spectroscopy is becoming a powerful tool for studying the phase-structure of such complex polymer systems as blends, filled, and reinforced materials. This way the dielectric technique is helpful in quality control even of such systems which are not used in the electrical or electronic industry.
